notes.1: Most candidates showed a good knowledge of the structure of an induction proof, though some did not communicate all the steps clearly. Sometimes the proposition was assumed for every integer and several candidates wrote 3k rather than 33k. Most manipulated the expressions well and better responses made the implication explicit in the final statement.
notes.2i: Most candidates drew the shape of the curve correctly and better responses showed the tangential nature of the graph at the pole.
notes.2iii: This part of the question was completed to a very high standard by the majority of candidates. Clear working was shown by most. Some preferred to write the expression in terms of the original variable rather than change the limits.
notes.3i: It was common to see all five fifth roots of unity written correctly. A few candidates gave only the arguments.
notes.3iii: Most candidates started the question successfully by solving a quadratic equation and finding the two values of z5. Better responses found the fifth roots of both the values and were able to write down all ten answers. Some insightful solutions were seen using de Moivre’s theorem to reduce the equation to 2cos5θ=−1.
notes.4i: Most candidates applied the method of differences correctly, showing enough working and terms to justify the given answer. A few candidates neglected to find the partial fractions before attempting to cancel terms. �PAGE�8
notes.4iii: Most candidates applied the result given in the previous part correctly. A few candidates chose to use the method of differences, again with mixed success. Some removed the N in the numerator or changed it to N2.
notes.5i: This part was generally well done and good knowledge of linear algebra was demonstrated.
notes.5iii: This part was also generally well done. A few candidates left their answer as a sum with two parameters, rather than writing down a basis.
notes.6i: With the exception of a small number of errors in division, the first part of the question was well done.
notes.6iii: Better responses produced well drawn and labelled sketches, showing correct forms at infinity, and curves approaching asymptotes. Some sketches had misplaced branches, but most did have the general shape correct.
notes.7i: The majority of candidates found the common perpendicular and applied the formula for the shortest distance accurately. A few responses took the longer approach of finding points of intersection with the common perpendicular which produced more errors.
notes.7iii: Most candidates knew how to find the angle required. They needed to adjust the answer they obtained, using the dot product correctly, to find the required angle.
notes.8: Almost all candidates knew how to approach this question and completed it to a high standard. There was some inaccuracy when solving linear equations to find the constants and some problems with notation. A few candidates used x as both a dependent and an independent variable, and some gave expressions instead of equations as their answer.
notes.9i: (ii) These parts were very well done by most candidates. They recalled the relationships between the roots and coefficients of the cubic equation and were able to use them accurately.
notes.9iiii: Those who used the cubic equation given in the question were usually successful, though a small number forgot to find S . Errors were seen when candidates did not recall the formula for ∑α3 correctly.
notes.9iv: The most common approach was to work with the product of roots, realising that complex roots occur in conjugate pairs. Some candidates did not specify that b is the real root.
notes.10i: (b) This was also completed to a very high standard with candidates going straight to the answer.
notes.10iii: There was less success in this part. Some responses unsuccessfully tried to use the answer to part
notes.10iiii: Most candidates realised the geometric nature of the series but some failed to recall the convergence condition correctly and 0<lna<1 was sometimes seen.
notes.10iv: The majority of candidates found the first derivative correctly using parametric differentiation. The attempts to find the second derivative varied greatly in length, with the better responses showing the required level of algebraic fluency and remembering to divide by after differentiating with respect to t. �PAGE�10

notes.general_comments:
The majority of candidates demonstrated very good knowledge across the whole syllabus. They showed
their working clearly and were accurate in their handling of algebra and calculus. They also showed
understanding of linear algebra. It seemed that all were able to complete the paper in the time allowed, and
the two options for Question 11 were equally popular.
